newsitem.title: USA: Group calls on AMA to give up seat in tobacco talks.
newsitem.headline: Group calls on AMA to give up seat in tobacco talks.

text.p: An activist physician's group said Tuesday the American Medical Association should give up its seat in settlement talks with the tobacco industry because of its alleged role in helping cover up the health effects of smoking in the early 1960s.

The group, citing court documents, said the AMA collaborated with the tobacco industry after accepting $18 million in research grants to study the effects of nicotine on smokers following release of the landmark 1964 Surgeon General's report on the dangers of smoking.

"There was a cover-up here the likes of which are comparable perhaps only with the Holocaust in Europe ... that allowed this industry to get away with murder," said Alan Blum, a professor at the Baylor College of Medicine and founder of the 2,000-member Doctors Ought to Care, or Doc.

Tobacco settlement negotiators in Washington were expected to make a last-ditch effort to reach a deal with the industry this week but were said to be at an impasse over liability issues, a source close to the talks said.

The AMA is represented in the negotiations by Lonnie Bristow, a former president who was tapped by public health groups to join the talks but criticized by anti-smoking groups for looking out for the interests of doctors over smokers.

Tom Houston, director of the AMA's department of preventive medicine and environmental health, defended Bristow as a strong proponent of tobacco controls and said he would not relinquish his role in the negotiations.
"The better part of valor is to be at the table, to understand what the talks are all about," Houston said. "For us to walk away from these negotiations, we think, would not be responsible."
Bristow could not be reached for comment.
Houston said the AMA in the late 1960s first passed a resolution that cigarette smoking was a cause of cancer, and has not covered up its earlier ties to the tobacco industry.

In 1964, the AMA opposed a Federal Trade Commission proposal to require warning labels on cigarettes, and much of the initial $10 million in industry grants went to members of its advisory board on smoking and health, according to documents produced by the tobacco industry in court cases.
"Unfortunately, we can't put that in context because the people working with that project are either dead or retired," Houston said. "There hasn't been any suppression of that information."
